title: Unclear units in chunk timing (section 13.3)
description:
Thanks for the great resource.

Section `13.3 Report how much time each chunk takes to run` provides a snippet to automatically print the executing time of code chunks. The current snippet only prints the number (with tons of decimals), without any unit (it's stripped out in the conversion to character of the `paste`), and the unit will be different between chunks (e.g. minutes when it's longer, seconds otherwise), leading to inconsistencies and confusion.

To avoid this, one options is to specify the unit when calculating the difference:
```
res <- difftime(Sys.time(), now, units="secs")
```
and then report it as such:
```
paste('Time for this code chunk to run:', round(res,2), 'seconds')
```

title: Document optional Pandoc packages
description:
[Pandoc's default LaTeX template](https://github.com/jgm/pandoc-templates/blob/2.14.1/default.latex) is clever: Some packages–as of v2.14.1 "upquote", "microtype", "parskip", "xurl", "bookmark" and "footnotehyper"–will only be used if they are available (checked via `\IfFileExists`). This way, however, they don't raise LaTeX error messages and `tinytex::parse_packages()` won't detect them.

Maybe the fact that optional packages won't be installed by the **tinytex** package should be documented somewhere? I am not sure where exactly this should go, mabye it's better suited in the **tinytex** documentation. Another option would be adding the packages in question to the [extended TinyTeX release](https://github.com/yihui/tinytex/blob/4c262cb/tools/pkgs-yihui.txt). (Or is there some other way that **tinytex** can actually detect these optional dependencies?)

title: Document that ONLY `bibliography` key implicitly triggers citeproc
description:
Only providing a bibliography via `pandoc_args` does not trigger citeproc:

``````Rmd
---
title: Test
output:
  html_document:
    pandoc_args: --bibliography=bibliography.bib
---

```{cat, engine.opts=list(file = "bibliography.bib")}
@Manual{Xie2020,
  title = {rmarkdown: Dynamic Documents for R},
  author = {JJ Allaire and Yihui Xie and Jonathan McPherson and
    Javier Luraschi and Kevin Ushey and Aron Atkins and Hadley
    Wickham and Joe Cheng and Winston Chang and Richard Iannone},
  year = {2020},
  note = {R package version 2.1},
  url = {https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown},
}
```

@Xie2020

``````

Only after providing the key `bibliography` in the metadata, it works:

``````Rmd
---
title: Test
output:
  html_document:
    pandoc_args: --bibliography=bibliography.bib
bibliography: ""
---

```{cat, engine.opts=list(file = "bibliography.bib")}
@Manual{Xie2020,
  title = {rmarkdown: Dynamic Documents for R},
  author = {JJ Allaire and Yihui Xie and Jonathan McPherson and
    Javier Luraschi and Kevin Ushey and Aron Atkins and Hadley
    Wickham and Joe Cheng and Winston Chang and Richard Iannone},
  year = {2020},
  note = {R package version 2.1},
  url = {https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown},
}
```

@Xie2020

``````

Alternatively (and more precise), one can could also provide `--citeproc` via `pandoc_args`.

I don't necessarily consider the described behaviour a bug, but documenting the fact that certain methods of providing a bibliography like `--bibliography` (or putting the `bibliography` key inside an external `--metadata-file`) do not (implicitly) trigger `--citeproc` might be helpful. Maybe in the section "[Bibliographies and citations](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/bibliography.html)" of the RMarkdown Cookbook.

title: A mistake in Chapter 17.5
description:
There is a mistake in the second code sample in Chapter 17.5:

```
#' Custom Knit function for RStudio
#'
#' @export
knit_with_date <- function(input, ...) {
  rmarkdown::render(
    input,
    output_file = paste0(
        xfun::sans_ext(input), '-', Sys.Date(), '.',
        xfun::file_ext(input)
    ),
    envir = globalenv()
  )
}
```

For input file `example.Rmd` on 2019-07-29 this function will output `example-2019-07-29.Rmd`.
There is no need to specify the file_ext for rmarkdown::render(). That is:

```
#' Custom Knit function for RStudio
#'
#' @export
knit_with_date <- function(input, ...) {
  rmarkdown::render(
    input,
    output_file = paste0(
      xfun::sans_ext(input), "-", Sys.Date()
    ),
    envir = globalenv()
  )
}
```

And I am not very clear about where to put `knit: myPackage::knit_with_date`, it worked when I put it in the header of my Rmd, but it said `argument "input" is missing, with no default` when I put it in `_output.yml` as below:

title: [Request] Font color modification with a Pandoc lua filter for Beamer and revealjs
description:
\* This is just a kind of feature request and not an urgent issue (Is it appropriate to post such a comment here on this GitHub repo?).

In the section you wrote about [the font colour modification with a Pandoc lua filter](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/font-color.html#lua-color), you included a lua filter which contains [the following line](https://github.com/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/blob/c603380774226d50f3501c17124bcea335e0a764/examples/font-color.Rmd#L28):

```lua
elseif FORMAT:match 'latex'
```

I would like to suggest that the following line would be more practical for those who want to knit with LaTeX/Beamer option than [the original script]((https://github.com/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/blob/c603380774226d50f3501c17124bcea335e0a764/examples/font-color.Rmd#L28)) I mentioned above: 

```lua
elseif FORMAT:match 'latex' or FORMAT:match 'beamer' then
```

(My example is inspired by [an answer on Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/a/63476966/10215301))

The motivation of my post here is that some `rmarkdown` beginners like me might wrongly think that LaTeX and Beamer are the same output format of Pandoc (or other relevant programmes), since Beamer is one of the `documentclass`es of LaTeX. However, actually these programmes treat Beamer as a different format from LaTeX and the original example is not applicable for Beamer output. 

The similar 'confusion' might occur when producing revealjs. So, [the line](https://github.com/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/blob/c603380774226d50f3501c17124bcea335e0a764/examples/font-color.Rmd#L21) can be replaced with:

```lua
if FORMAT:match 'html' or FORMAT:match 'revealjs' then
```

as the ansewerer of the SO post I linked here suggests.

title: Mention yaml tag !expr to set some metadata programmatically
description:
Considering the similarity, I would mention the possibility to use the special yaml tag `!expr` as an alternative to `knitr`'s inline code (discussed [here](https://github.com/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/blob/1d95296/04-content.Rmd#L65-L78)). The former is provided by the `yaml` package and works when the latter doesn't, such as in the `output` or `params` settings, and vice versa:

``````Rmd
---
params:
  doc_title: !expr format(Sys.time(), format='Report from %A')
  doc_author: !expr Sys.getenv('USER')
title: "`r params$doc_title`"
author: "`r params$doc_author`"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output:
  html_document:
    theme: !expr sample(c('yeti', 'united', 'lumen'), 1)
---

```{r, binder, echo = FALSE, results='asis'}
if (identical(params$doc_author, "jovyan")) {
  cat("Flying through Jupyter’s orbit")
}
```

``````

Writing

- ``"`r sample(c('yeti', 'united', 'lumen'), 1)`"`` instead of `!expr sample(c('yeti', 'united', 'lumen'), 1)`
- ``"`r Sys.getenv('USER')`"`` instead of `!expr Sys.getenv('USER')` or
- `!expr Sys.Date()` instead of ``"`r Sys.Date()`"``

would not lead to the desired outcome.

Also, only yaml expressions can be used to populate fields: Writing `rmarkdown::metadata$author` instead of `params$doc_author` in the chunk `binder` wouldn't work (at least without wrapping it into `knitr::knit`).

Finally, `params` (the list of parameters provided within the knitting environment) is not available for yaml expressions.

See further rstudio/rmarkdown#1387

__Edit__ (2020-09-06): `knitr`'s `!r` syntax could be mentioned alongside:

``````Rmd
---
title: My Document
output: html_document
params:
  date: !r Sys.Date()
---

``````

[Inline code](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/r-code.html), [`!expr`](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/output-formats.html) and [`!r`](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/params-declare.html) are all covered in the R Markdown Guide, but it might make sense to compare them in one place.

__Edit__ (2020-10-07): The Rmd document above will not compile if `params$doc_title` contains double quotes (`"`). Therefore it may be appropriate to write something like

```yaml
title: "`r gsub('\"', '\\\\\"', params$doc_title)`"
```

description:
From John: 

> Please send me six key words or phrases that will improve search results. Do not repeat words in the title as they are already included.

title: Write back cover copy
description:
Back-cover copy should not exceed 350 words. Because this copy will be made available to search
engines, there are some important guidelines:

1. The first few sentences will have the greatest impact.
2. Discuss your book, not the area.
3. When you list a feature, include the benefit or why a reader would want this feature.
4. Use key words in the book title, chapter titles, and the back-cover copy. If you were looking for a book
in this area, what words would you include in your search? Avoid being cute if that means using words
you would not use while searching.
5. If this is a new edition, describe what is new.

The first paragraph states what type of book this is, what is distinctive, and what the prerequisites are. Try
to include what is distinctive in the first sentence. Explain how your book helps the audience solve a
specific problem and this will make the audience clear. A potential reader does not need general
information about the field.

The second paragraph give more details. You can also state what the benefits are; after reading chapters,
what will you be able to do that you previously could not. You can use paragraphs or bullets. Include
what supplements or web materials will be available.

The third paragraph in a few sentences provides biographical details that establish you as an authority in
this area. Include your name, title, affiliation, and any impressive facts. What are your main research
areas, have you edited any journals, won any prizes, published other books, or taught online or short
courses? Details about your Ph.D. or visiting positions usually should not be included.

Note on the preface: If you will offer supplementary material on a website, try to include your address
and ours. Ours may be more stable and we can change our link to your site if necessary.

title: Custom output function
description:
I know that `R Markdown: The Definitive Guide` explains that users can create and call custom output functions (https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/format-derive.html). However, I wonder if it would be worth adding a recipe to re-emphasize this point in this book?

A number of the individual recipes (e.g. custom style sheet, custom footer, etc.) are items that could be included in such a function. In my experience, most of the times I have edited these options, I have done it for tasks I will want to repeat (e.g. making a few corporate-themed formats.) 

Thus, it might be nice to show users how to piece together other recipes into their own function / package. I think the bigger "trick" here is simply knowing where one can store the necessary resources (in the `inst/` folder) and how to access them (with `system.file`).

title: Font color section - alternative solution which allows markdown syntax
description: Hi Yihui! I read the section on [Font color](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown-cookbook/font-color.html) because I grappled with this in the [`oxforddown`](https://github.com/ulyngs/oxforddown) package... The solution provided in the section is this: ```r colorize <- function(x, color) { if (knitr::is_latex_output()) { sprintf("\\textcolor{%s}{%s}", color, x) } else if (knitr::is_html_output()) { sprintf("%s", color, x) } else x } ``` However, this doesn't allow for use of markdown syntax within coloured text. For example `` Test this `r colorize("will actually do *what* I want", "red")` will it? `` renders the asterisks as literal asterisks in PDF output: I described a solution in [this blog post](https://ulriklyngs.com/post/2019/02/20/how-to-use-pandoc-filters-for-advanced-customisation-of-your-r-markdown-documents/) which uses span elements: **color_filter.lua**: ```lua function Span (el) if el.classes[1] == "textcolor-red" then table.insert(el.content, 1, pandoc.RawInline('latex', '\\textcolor{red}{')) table.insert(el.content, pandoc.RawInline('latex', '}')) end return el.content end ``` **style.css**: ```css .textcolor-red { color: red; } ``` **test.Rmd**: ```markdown --- output: pdf_document: extra_dependencies: ["xcolor"] pandoc_args: ["--lua-filter=color_filter.lua"] html_document: css: style.css --- Roses are red and *italicised* and violets aren't. ``` Perhaps this would be helpful to include? :)

title: Some tips and conventions on authoring the book (for co-authors of this book)
description:
I just finished reading the current draft. I think I have to remind you of a boring yet important task: since the book is meant to be printed with a relatively small page width, we will have to make sure the images are clearly readable and the verbatim examples won't reach the page margin. For example, the font size in [Figure 4.1](https://dr-harper.github.io/rmarkdown-cookbook/crossRef.html) is way too small:

![](https://dr-harper.github.io/rmarkdown-cookbook/images/crossReferencing.png)

(In fact, this particular figure would be better if it has a frame, otherwise it can confusing to readers because they may not be able to tell the difference between the text in the book and the text in the figure. When the image doesn't have a clear border, I'll manually add one, such as Figure 6.1 in the R Markdown book: https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/tufte-handouts.html. The ImageMagick command I used was `convert INPUT -shave 1x1 -bordercolor black -border 1 OUTPUT`.)

And the example text in Section 11.2.1 is too wide:

```
# About

This analysis was written in the R programming language [@R-base]. The report was generated using **rmarkdown** [@R-markdown] and **knitr** [@R-knitr].
```

We need to try our best to keep the line width under 70 characters. Sometimes it is hard to fit even one extra character: https://github.com/rstudio/blogdown/pull/399

The same issue exists in tables. In general, try your very best to keep the text short in tables, e.g.

- https://bookdown.org/yihui/blogdown/global-options.html
- https://bookdown.org/yihui/blogdown/more-global-options.html

It is not trivially simple to decide the best column widths to wrap long text. I have used extremely ugly hacks ([that you probably don't want to see](https://github.com/rstudio/rmarkdown-book/blob/612703943c676ad6f2572c1568b6cd61f5970ab6/index.Rmd#L40-L43)) to fix [certain tables](https://bookdown.org/yihui/rmarkdown/htmlwidgets-size.html#tab:sizing-policy) in my previous books.

I'll work on the PDF output next (with the Chapman & Hall style), and will have a better idea which elements need to be fixed.

BTW, for optimizing images, to keep the repo lean in file size, I wish you could optimize them locally before pushing to Github (then rely on a Github bot to optimize them and send pull requests, which will inflate the size of the repo). I have a helper function `xfun::optipng()` to do that if you have installed `optipng`. I kind of have an OCD on this. All images in my previous books were heavily optimized before I commit them because I don't like version control binary files in general. I not only run `optipng` but also use https://imagecompressor.com to further optimize them as much as possible, to the point where I feel the loss of quality is noticeable.

title: How to change knitr options at rendering ?
description:
Not sure it is well known, even if it is in the doc but you can change knitr options with `knitr.package.<option>` in `options` like with `options(knitr.package.progress = FALSE)`

This could be very useful for changing something default at rendering, setting such an option before `render()` i.e in `_travis.yml`

```sh
script:
- Rscript -e 'options(knitr.package.progress = FALSE);bookdown::render_book("index.Rmd")'
```

It will work only if this options is not override inside the project.

title: A trick to reuse some code in an Rmarkdown, like ggplot theme
description:
This comes from https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/083-ggplot2-reference.Rmd and I did not know about that 

````markdown
# Externalize ggplot2 code
 
You may have your own layout code like [this one](http://stackoverflow.com/q/14802183/559676), and you do not want to type the code again and again. One way to avoid repeating the code explicitly is to use chunk references. Although **knitr** is based on the idea of literate programming, but we rarely need programming, and this is one case in which literate programming may be helpful.

We simplify the layout code in the original post and put it in a code chunk named `my-layout`:

```{r my-layout, eval=FALSE}
theme (legend.text = element_text(size = 12, angle=45))+
  theme (legend.position = "bottom")
```

Now we can use `<<>>` to reference it.

```{r test-a}
library(ggplot2)
qplot(carat, price, data=diamonds, color=cut)+
  <<my-layout>>
```

Another test:

```{r test-b, message=FALSE}
qplot(carat, data=diamonds, fill=cut)+
  <<my-layout>>
```
````

title: How to add an item to bibliography without using it
description:
See this question
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/32946203/including-bibliography-in-rmarkdown-document-with-use-of-the-knitcitations

This is a pandoc feature
> If you want to include items in the bibliography without actually citing them in the body text, you can define a dummy nocite metadata field and put the citations there:
> ```` 
> ---
>nocite: |
>  @item1, @item2
>...
> 
>@item3
> ````
> In this example, the document will contain a citation for item3 only, but the bibliography will contain entries for item1, item2, and item3.

Exemple from a QA answer 
```````r
````{r img-setup, include=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
out.format <- knitr::opts_knit$get("out.format")
img_template <- switch( out.format,
                     word = list("img-params"=list(fig.width=6,
                                                   fig.height=6,
                                                   dpi=150)),
                     {
                       # default
                       list("img-params"=list( dpi=150,
                                               fig.width=6,
                                               fig.height=6,
                                               out.width="504px",
                                               out.height="504px"))
                     } )

knitr::opts_template$set( img_template )
````

title: How to customize code chunks ouputs ?
description:
We could have some recipes on how to customize code chunk output.
The idea is to talk about
* Replacing all the higlighting: using `highlight: null` and provide a custome css with the tags used for highligting (https://github.com/jeffbr13/benjeffrey.com/blob/master/posts/pandoc-syntax-highlighting-css.md)
```css
code > span.kw { color: #555; font-weight: bold; } /* Keyword */
code > span.dt { color: #902000; } /* DataType */
code > span.dv { color: #40a070; } /* DecVal (decimal values) */
code > span.bn { color: #d14; } /* BaseN */
code > span.fl { color: #d14; } /* Float */
code > span.ch { color: #d14; } /* Char */
code > span.st { color: #d14; } /* String */
code > span.co { color: #888888; font-style: italic; } /* Comment */
code > span.ot { color: #007020; } /* OtherToken */
code > span.al { color: #ff0000; font-weight: bold; } /* AlertToken */
code > span.fu { color: #900; font-weight: bold; } /* Function calls */
code > span.er { color: #a61717; background-color: #e3d2d2; } /* ErrorTok */
```
* Apply custom formatting on a chunk basis using knitr `class.source` or `class.output` options and a CSS
* deactivate highlighting with `highlight=FALSE` chunk option
* Do not touch the highlighting but other style of the code chunk using by modifying with css html tag `pre`, `code` and/or class `.r` or others languages. 

Also
* Background color in latex through `background` chunk option
I would find it useful to have all this in a cookbook to go from time to time as it is not well known I think.

title: How to add numbered figure caption in a document ?
description:
This is an old question than know have an answer with bookdown, but can also be dealt without it. Should both be mentionned ? 

## with bookdown 
**Easiest solution**
Automatic numbering and cross referencing
https://bookdown.org/yihui/bookdown/a-single-document.html

## without bookdown
It is possible to number figure and add caption without bookdown.
* Use a custom function and `fig.cap` chunk option
````r
# Incremental Figure Numbers

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
fn = local({
  i = 0
  function(x) {
    i <<- i + 1
    paste('Figure ', i, ': ', x, sep = '')
  }
})
```

```{r test-a, fig.cap=fn('this is one plot')}
plot(1:10)
```

```{r test-b, fig.cap=fn('another plot')}
plot(rnorm(10))
```
````
Source : [knitr example](https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/070-caption-num.Rmd)

title: Provide examples or better documentation on creating new rmarkdown themes
description:
One thing I found that may need some extensive discussions in the definitive guide is how to create new templates from rmarkdown (Chapter 17/18). I'm thinking it would be nice to have a longer chapter talking about how to create a new rmarkdown template under different settings. For example, how to create HTML template with/without bootstrap or how to merge existing LaTeX template with the default pandoc template (like how to understand the syntax in the pandoc latex template file). 

I feel like there are definitely people who have the intention to create new themes for their workplace but they are stopped by the lack of good tutorials on this topic. Also, I sort of get a feeling that there are lots of good templates out there but they are not converted to a rmarkdown-compatible formats. If there are more people who can learn how to do these customizations, I bet @yihui will be happy to get more submissions on themes in future bookdown contests. lol

title: Clarify structure of book
description:
I am keen to set this project up to make it easy for others to contribute to. A big part of this is trying to clarify the exact purpose of the book, and a general structure of the book chapters and content.

My initial thoughts would be that the book would offer some examples of how to extend R Markdown, with useful tips and tricks for intermediate/advanced users. It would be aimed at people who had read the R Markdown Definitive Guide so skip a lot of the basics often covered in R Markdown guides (markdown syntax etc.).

You can see I have tried to establish a structure for the overall book of things I think are worth covering, but again these are fairly adaptable and open to amendments.
